readerTitle: The deal you won from the buyer and lost to the users
caseNote: 가상 사례 (호텔 그룹에 조리복을 납품하는 업체, 제빵 장비, 경비 정산 소프트웨어) · 모든 상황과 수치는 설명용
insight: 기업 고객에게는 계약서에 서명하는 사람과 매일 그 제품을 쓰는 사람이 따로 있다. 첫 판매는 구매자가 정하지만, 재계약은 사용자가 정할 때가 많다.
misconception: 계약서에 서명하는 사람을 설득하면 판매는 끝난 것이다.

sources.text: B2B 마케팅의 표준 개념 (구매 의사결정 단위에서 구매자 buyer와 사용자 user의 역할 구분)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례는 가상입니다. 조리복 업체의 '15% 저렴', 경비 정산 소프트웨어의 '300명 중 약 20% 사용' 같은 수치는 설명용이며 실제 통계가 아닙니다.
BMO-01-02(사용자 vs 지불자)와 겹치지 않는지 확인하세요. 이 레슨은 기업 구매 상황에서 구매 담당자와 현장 사용자의 차이를 다루고, 구매위원회 전체는 CUS-09-02로 넘깁니다.

cards.title: The deal you won from the buyer and lost to the users
body: A uniform supplier wins a three-year contract to dress the cooks at a hotel group's twelve kitchens. Its price is 15% below the old supplier's, and the purchasing team is delighted.
The cooks wear the new jackets for one shift. Then the complaints start.

image.label: A purchasing manager smiling at a contract while cooks sweat in a hot kitchen
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽은 시원한 사무실에서 계약서에 서명하며 웃는 구매 담당자, 오른쪽은 뜨거운 주방에서 새 조리복을 입고 땀 흘리며 옷깃을 당기는 요리사들. 실제 호텔이나 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where do you spend your sales time?
body: You're the uniform supplier. The hotel group's purchasing manager runs the tender. She cares most about price, delivery terms and one invoice for all twelve sites.
You have two weeks before the offer is due. Where do you put most of your effort?

options.text: Sharpen the price and terms for the purchasing manager
options.feedback: You may win the contract. But you learn nothing about the people who will wear the jackets for ten hours a day, and they will judge you at renewal.

options.text: Spend a day in two kitchens, test jackets with cooks, and build their needs into the offer
options.feedback: You give up some time on the price sheet. In return, the offer works for the person who signs and for the people who wear it.

options.text: Win on price now, then fix any complaints after the contract starts
options.feedback: Fixing problems later is better than ignoring them. But once cooks decide your jackets are bad, changing their minds costs more than asking them first.

cards.title: Cheaper on paper, unbearable at the stove.
body: The supplier chose option A. The cheaper jackets used a heavier fabric that trapped heat. Cooks started buying their own jackets and wearing them instead.
Head chefs complained to their general managers. When the contract came up for renewal, the chefs had a favorite supplier ready. Purchasing switched.
The supplier had sold to the right person and still lost the customer.

cards.title: Buyers vs users
body: In business buying, the **buyer** chooses and pays. The **user** lives with the product every day. They are often different people, and they measure success differently.
The buyer asks: is the price fair, are the terms safe, does it fit the budget? The user asks: does this make my work easier or harder?
The buyer usually decides the first sale. The users often decide whether there is a second one.

image.label: Two people looking at the same product through different lenses
image.brief: 한 제품(조리복)을 가운데 두고 양쪽에 두 사람. 왼쪽 구매자의 말풍선에는 "Price · Terms · Budget", 오른쪽 사용자의 말풍선에는 "Comfort · Speed · Daily hassle". 깔끔한 인포그래픽 스타일.

cards.title: Map the people around one purchase.
body: Before you pitch a business customer, find out who fills each role:
list: **Who pays:** whose budget the money comes from
**Who signs:** who has the authority to say yes
**Who feels the results:** who notices if it works or fails
cards.callout: When one person fills every role, sell to that person. When the roles split, each one needs its own reason to say yes.

cards.title: Users who love you can't sign the check.
body: The mistake runs both ways. Picture a bakery chain whose bakers love a new dough mixer. It's quieter and easier to clean. The finance director sees only a price that is double the old one, and says no.
Users can pull for you, but they rarely hold the budget. The fix is to translate their gains into the buyer's language: minutes saved per batch, fewer repairs, less wasted dough.

cards.title: Serving users doesn't mean going around the buyer.
body: Pitching staff behind the buyer's back can damage trust. Ask the buyer for access to users, and share what you learn.
Users don't always know best either. They may resist any change, even a good one. Listen for the problems behind their complaints.
And in a small business, the owner may be buyer and user at once. Map the roles before assuming they split.

cards.title: Now it's expense software.
body: You sell expense-report software. A 300-person company's finance director signed a one-year deal. Three months in, only about 20% of employees submit expenses through it. The rest still email spreadsheets.
Renewal is nine months away. What do you do?

options.text: Send the finance director a usage report and ask her to make the tool mandatory
options.feedback: A rule can raise usage fast. But users forced into a tool they dislike will keep complaining, and that noise reaches the director before renewal.

options.text: Watch a few employees file expenses, fix the steps that annoy them, then show the director the gains
options.feedback: It takes more work now. You win the users who decide adoption and give the buyer proof she chose well.

options.text: Offer a discount at renewal to keep the account
options.feedback: You may keep the deal for another year, at a lower price. The real problem, users who don't want the product, is still there.

cards.title: The buyer signs once. The users decide every day.
body: With business customers, win the person who pays and the people who use it. Each needs a different reason to say yes.
**Try it today:** pick your biggest business customer. Write down who signed, and name one person who uses your product daily. When did you last talk to that person?
